newsitem.title: DUBAI: Expanded Saudi body still seen far from democracy.
newsitem.headline: Expanded Saudi body still seen far from democracy.

text.p: The expansion of Saudi Arabia's consultative Shura Council will increase popular input in the country's affairs, but analysts say the body is still a far cry from Western concepts of democracy.

The kingdom on Sunday raised the number of members in the country's only representative assembly to 90 from 60, including active and retired military officers, senior government officials, business executives, members of large tribes and the Shi'ite Moslem minority.
Thirty of the original 60 members appointed when the all-male council was inaugurated in 1993 were also replaced.
King Fahd told the weekly cabinet meeting on Monday the move would support Saudi development and ensure an adequate number of experts advised the government on a wide range of issues.
Diplomats in the kingdom said it was difficult to gauge what impact the body's new make-up would have on the political reforms Saudi Arabia introduced more than three years ago.
"The expansion shows that the government is taking the council and its views seriously," a Western diplomat told Reuters by telephone from Riyadh.
"But don't confuse the council with a Western-style parliament," he said. "It's not elected. It can't make laws. It just discusses issues the government has asked them to discuss."

The king, 75 this year, promised after the 1990-91 Gulf crisis to gradually introduce political and economic reforms aimed at modernising the system of government in the world's biggest oil producer and exporter.

In December 1993 he launched the Shura Council, the country's first representative body for almost 60 years, and set up regional assemblies in 13 provinces, fledgling steps towards giving Saudis more say in running the country's affairs.

The Shura has a purely advisory function and decision-making rests with the government. Senior members of the Saudi royal family traditionally control the country's administration, holding many top positions at a national and regional level.

The 1993 moves were denounced by some in the West as too shallow, but at home they were widely welcomed as stepping stones to more popular participation. Saudi scholars said there were many different kinds of democracy, stressing the Western and Islamic variants could not be compared.

"The council is respected by both the government and the people," one senior Western diplomat said. "Because the Shura members are not from the royal family but the population at large, they are in tune with popular sentiment."
Other diplomats said the council's broad membership base brought together the know-how of the country's elite while providing a good sounding board for the government.

Some said the expansion also sought to grant the minority Shi'ite population a greater say. Saudi Arabia, which enforces Islamic Sharia law, is predominantly Sunni Moslem. Diplomats said there were two or three Shi'ites in the new council up from one in the previous body.

Council President Sheikh Mohammad bin Jubair, a Sunni scholar and former justice minister, was reappointed for a second term. Analysts said that while a number of religious figures had been appointed to the expanded council, the religious establishment had hoped for wider representation.
Diplomats across the board said the expansion would help reforms but said the effect would not be felt overnight.
"This is not a dramatic move," a senior diplomat said. "It won't make much of a difference but it will expand the consultative base, if only within a modest framework."
